definition: Disproportionately means out of proportion — to a degree far larger or smaller than the comparison it sits beside would justify.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word disproportionately. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know disproportionately should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Although seniors cast only a fifth of the votes, they appear disproportionately in the exit polls, filling nearly half the sample.
Unevenly is milder than disproportionately: uneven means the shares merely differ, while disproportionately means the difference has broken the ratio that fairness or arithmetic would predict.
Overwhelmingly outdoes disproportionately: a cost can fall disproportionately on renters at twice their fair share, but overwhelmingly means the imbalance has crowded out nearly everyone else's part.
Excessively means more than is reasonable in itself; disproportionately always measures against something else — a share, a cause, a group's size — and finds the ratio wrong.
Unduly means more than is fair or warranted; unduly passes a quiet judgment, while disproportionately states the arithmetic — this piece is too big for that whole.
Unevenly means without uniformity, in an irregular pattern; a coat of paint dries unevenly, but only when one share is wrong against another does disproportionately apply.

Disproportionately means out of proportion — to a degree far larger or smaller than the comparison it sits beside would justify.
The audit found that late fees fell disproportionately on the branch's smallest accounts: customers holding two percent of the deposits were paying forty percent of the penalties.
Two percent of the money, forty percent of the fees — the shares are wildly out of step, and disproportionately is the adverb that flags exactly that broken ratio.
The word never judges an amount on its own; it always compares a share against the whole it came from.
Disproportionately is the adverb of audits and headlines, and it comes with homework: name the ratio, or the word is just noise.
'Fees fell disproportionately on small accounts' earns its keep only when the reader learns the shares.
It runs both directions — a group can be disproportionately harmed or disproportionately rewarded.

When the library finally studied its overdue fines, one finding startled the board: the fines fell disproportionately on the youngest cardholders.
Children held fewer than a quarter of the library's cards.
Yet their accounts carried more than two thirds of all blocked-card penalties.
The librarians could name the reasons -- school schedules, rides that never came, books lost in shared bedrooms.
The fix was simpler than the study.
Fines on children's cards ended that spring, and the books, the data later showed, came back anyway.
